title: Scale behavior sandbox: multi-region prewarm + predictive triggers (May 2025)
content:
Overview and purpose:

Notes from sandbox runs exploring how our autoscaler behaves when 1) workloads span 2 regions with different GPU mixes (A100-80GB in us-west, H100-80GB in eu-west), and 2) we introduce a small predictive layer to prewarm capacity for expected spike windows. Goal: find simple, low-friction policy knobs that reduce p99 token latency violations during 5–10x short spikes while containing cost uplift to <12% relative to baseline reactive autoscale.

High-level experiment design (rough):
- Traffic shape: baseline steady 200 requests/min (avg seq len 128), with synthetic spike windows: 3x (5m), 5x (1m), and 10x (30s) at random times in a 6-hour test window.
- Regions: us-west (A100 pool, 64 GPUs), eu-west (H100 pool, 32 GPUs) — tests run with cross-region routing enabled (soft affinity).
- Policies tested: 1) reactive (util > 70% -> scale out), 2) reactive + cooldown jitter, 3) reactive + min_per_region, 4) predictive prewarm (simple EWMA traffic forecast per 5m bucket) + reactive fallback, 5) burst buffer (reserved 10% burst capacity per region).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 tok latency, scale latency (time GPU added and ready), cost delta (estimated), scale churn (#scale events), percent of requests falling back to lower-tier model.

Representative config snippets used in sandbox (pseudo-format):
- policy A (reactive default):
  min_instances: 2
  max_instances: 60
  scale_out_threshold: 0.70
  scale_in_threshold: 0.30
  cooldown: 120s

- policy B (min per region):
  min_per_region: {us-west: 6, eu-west: 3}
  max_instances: 60
  scale_out_threshold: 0.75
  cooldown: 90s

- policy C (predictive prewarm + reactive):
  predictive_window: 5m
  forecast_method: EWMA(alpha=0.4)
  prewarm_margin: +20% of forecast
  reactive_threshold: 0.80
  prewarm_lead: 90s
  max_prewarm_cap: 10% of region pool

Key observations (empirical):
- Reactive-only (policy A) handled gradual load increases well but consistently failed on 30s 10x spikes: median scale-out time to first usable GPU was ~48s (provision+container pull+model load = 40–60s depending on region), resulting in 40–60% p99 latency violations during spikes.
- Adding cooldown jitter reduced synchronous scale-in storms but did not materially improve spike handling.
- min_per_region (policy B) significantly reduced cross-region cold-starts for routed requests: where previously eu-west saw 70% cold-start fallback when a spike was routed there, with min_per_region it fell to <10%. Cost uplift measured ~+6% vs baseline because we kept warm capacity idle between spikes.
- Predictive prewarm (policy C) cut p99 violations in half for 1m and 5m spikes when forecasts were accurate. Two failure modes: 1) forecast misses (sudden, unpredicted spikes) — predictive layer introduced extra complexity but fell back to reactive; 2) overforecasting for low-signal traffic (resulted in unnecessary prewarm cost). Overall cost delta ~+9% for tuned alpha=0.4 and prewarm_margin=20%.
- Burst buffer (reserved 10% pool) was simple to reason about and gave most consistent user-visible latency wins for micro-spikes but at a higher steady cost (+11–14%).

Quantitative summary (representative numbers from one 6-hour run):
- Policy A (reactive): p99 spike violation rate 0.37 (37% of spike windows had p99 > SLO), cost delta +0% (baseline), average scale latency 48s
- Policy B (min_per_region): p99 violation rate 0.12, cost delta +6%, avg scale latency 30s
- Policy C (predictive+reactive): p99 violation rate 0.06, cost delta +9%, avg scale latency 22s (when forecast correct), 52s when forecast missed
- Policy D (burst buffer 10%): p99 violation rate 0.03, cost delta +12.5%, avg scale latency 8s

Operational notes and caveats:
- Model load time dominates scale latency. For many of our larger models (30B+), model load contributes ~30–45s. If we can split warm cache vs model weights (e.g., keep KV cache warm but lazy load weights) we could change the tradeoffs here.
- Cross-region routing adds another failure mode: if a region is saturated and routing shifts traffic, the receiving region must have headroom or prewarm in place. min_per_region + soft-affinity routing gives best guarantees for region-local latencies.
- Cold-start variability between clouds/regions: eu-west pulls container images ~20% slower due to repo mirror lag; accounted for in experiments by adding an extra 10s penalty in eu-west runs.
- Prediction reliability is traffic dependent. For customer A/B tests with clear daily patterns (diurnal + predictable spikes), predictive prewarm performed great. For spiky, bursty workloads (e.g., submit-once CI or bulk ingestion) predictive layer often overfit and cost more.

Recommendations (practical policy suggestions to test next):
1) Rollout min_per_region as a conservative default for multi-region customers: set to 5% of region pool or absolute floor (us-west: 6, eu-west: 3) depending on SLA tier. Document cost impact and allow customers to opt out.
2) Offer predictive prewarm as an opt-in addon: keep the algorithm simple (EWMA per 5m with conservative margins) and surface forecast confidence and recent accuracy in the Console.
3) Implement a small burst buffer option (config toggle) that reserves N GPUs per region for low-latency micro-spikes — clearly call out cost+benefit.
4) Work on reducing model load time (engine work): explore fast snapshot/weight streaming, or lightweight warm containers that retain weight artifacts between requests.
5) Improve observability: add per-region scale-latency breakdown, per-policy forecast-vs-actual chart, and an alert when forecast miss rate > 25% over 24h.

Open questions / experiments to run next (todo backlog):
- Evaluate hybrid approach: small burst buffer + predictive prewarm for enterprise accounts — is there a sweet spot for cost vs p99?
- Test different forecast methods (simple Prophet/seasonal for customers with daily patterns) vs EWMA; measure calibration overhead.
- Auto-tune prewarm_margin based on recent forecast error (e.g., margin = min(50%, 2*RMSE_rel)).
- Decompose model load: can we shift to a two-stage readiness (inference runtime ready but weights streaming) to lower observed p99 during cold start?

Notes to self / reminders:
- Attach raw run logs and pod lifecycle traces to RED-456 for follow-up.
- Sync with solutions-eng on customer-facing language: they want an easy checkbox for "low-latency spikes" in the Console; need to produce cost estimator UX copy.
- Consider running an on-customer A/B with Product for a mid-market customer that has predictable daily spikes (ask Aisha to propose candidates).

Appendix: sample raw trace excerpt (one 10s slice, simplified):
- t=00:00:00 request spike start -> routed to eu-west (no warm node)
- t=00:00:10 autoscaler starts provisioning new GPU node
- t=00:00:30 node registers, container pulls start
- t=00:00:55 model loaded and ready -> first warmed responses at t=00:00:56
- observed p99 latency in that slice: 14.2s

Contact / owners for follow-up: Leah Park (infra), Mateo Ruiz (serving runtime), Aisha Khan (product), Connor Li (SRE).

End notes: this doc is a working sandbox dump — contains rough numbers from a small number of runs. Purpose is to capture intuition, configs that seemed promising, and prioritized next steps. Will convert into a more structured playbook if we converge on policy knobs.
